'''Apalachee''' was a [[Muskogean language]] of [[Florida]]. It was closely related to [[Koasati language|Koasati]] and [[Alabama language|Alabama]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Broadwell |first1=George A. |title=Reconstructing Proto-Muskogean Language and Prehistory: Preliminary results |date=1992 |citeseerx=10.1.1.72.4700 |at=3, en. 2}}</ref> Apalachee was found to belong to the same branch of the Muskogean family as Koasati, Alabama, and [[Hitchiti_language|Hitchiti]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Haas |first1=Mary R. |author1-link=Mary Haas |title=The Position of Apalachee in the Muskogean Family |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |date=April 1949 |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=121–127 |doi=10.1086/464031 |publisher=University of Chicago Press}}</ref> Apalachee was originally spoken in western Florida, but is believed to have last been spoken in the nineteenth century by [[Apalachee|Apalachee people]] that had been [[indian removal|removed]] to Louisiana.<ref name="Goddard2005">{{cite journal |last1=Goddard |first1=Ives |title=The Indigenous Languages of the Southeast |journal=Anthropological Linguistics |date=2005 |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=1–60 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25132315 |access-date=18 May 2026 |issn=0003-5483}}</ref>{{rp|11}}

==History==
The language is known primarily from one document, a letter written in 1688 to [[Charles II of Spain]]. The original version of that letter is lost, but a copy published in 1860 survives. Additional Apalachee texts are said to have existed in archives in Havana but they have never been located.<ref name=Kimball1987>{{cite journal |last1=Kimball |first1=Geoffrey |title=A Grammatical Sketch of Apalachee |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |date=April 1987 |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=136–174 |doi=10.1086/466050 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |jstor=1265142}}</ref>{{rp|136}} 

The letter is accompanied by a loose Spanish translation, from which some aspects of Apalachee have been inferred. Related Muskogean languages have also been used to help understand the structure of Apalachee.<ref name=Kimball1987/>{{rp|136-137}}<ref name=Kimball1988>{{cite journal |last1=Kimball |first1=Geoffrey |title=An Apalachee Vocabulary |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |date=October 1988 |volume=54 |issue=4 |pages=387–398 |doi=10.1086/466093 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |jstor=1265100}}</ref>{{rp|388}} Geoffrey Kimball produced a grammatical sketch<ref name=Kimball1987/> and a vocabulary of the language<ref name=Kimball1988/> based on these resources.

Apalachee is one of only three indigenous languages from its region to have any surviving documentation, alongside [[Timucua language|Timucua]] and [[Calusa language|Calusa]].<ref name=Goddard2005/>{{rp|28}}

==Grammar==
Apalachee relies on fixed [[word order]] ([[Subject–object–verb word order|subject–object–verb]]) rather than [[Grammatical case|case marking]] to specify the subject and object of a sentence. Apalachee does have some case markings, but does not rely on them to the same degree that other Muskogean languages do.<ref name=Kimball1987/>{{rp|139}}

There is significant [[Affix|affixation]] in Apalachee morphology. Possession and pluralization are both marked by affixes on the noun. Objects can be marked on the verbs by prefixes.<ref name=Kimball1987/>{{rp|140-141,147}} Derivational affixes are attested for both nouns and verbs, including distributive and causative markers.<ref name=Kimball1987/>{{rp|153,156}}
